concepts.title: Upserts, Updates, and Deletes in a Vector Index
concepts.description: Vector indexes are built and tuned for fast querying, not for the kind of cheap, instantaneous row-level edits a relational database offers for free; understanding how upserts, metadata patches, and deletes actually work underneath -- tombstones, staged compaction, re-embedding on content change -- is what keeps a production index correct and fast as data churns.
learningObjectives: Explain why removing a vector from a graph-based ANN index (HNSW) is structurally harder than deleting a row from a table, and what problem a tombstone solves.
Distinguish a metadata-only update from a vector-content update, and explain why the former is cheap while the latter requires re-embedding and re-inserting the vector itself.
Define upsert semantics (insert-or-update keyed by a stable ID) and explain why an ID-less append can silently create duplicate, stale entries instead of updating in place.
Explain why tombstone accumulation degrades query latency and memory footprint over time, and why periodic compaction or a full rebuild is required to reclaim that cost.
Debug a system where document content changed but the stored vector did not, and explain why that failure is silent rather than an error.

sections.heading: Why Vector Indexes Resist Being Edited
sections.body:
A relational database is built around the assumption that rows get updated and deleted constantly, cheaply, and in isolation from one another -- `UPDATE` and `DELETE` are first-class, fast operations precisely because a row's storage doesn't depend on any other row's storage. An ANN index makes almost the opposite bet: HNSW's entire speed advantage comes from a carefully built graph where each node's edges were chosen specifically because of that node's position relative to its neighbors at build time, and IVF's speed advantage comes from centroids computed once, offline, over the whole collection as it existed at clustering time. Both structures are optimized for read (query) performance by doing real, structural work up front -- and that same work is exactly what makes them expensive to edit later.

Concretely: removing a single vector from an HNSW graph isn't just deleting one node -- it potentially orphans the *other* nodes that relied on it as a bridge between two regions of the graph. If node X was the only connection linking a dense cluster of documents about one topic to the rest of the graph, deleting X on the spot means re-examining and re-linking every one of X's neighbors so the graph stays fully navigable, which is real, non-trivial work to do correctly, and doing it synchronously on every single delete would make deletes as slow as a partial rebuild. IVF has a milder version of the same problem: removing a vector from a cluster is cheap by itself (just drop it from that cluster's list), but the cluster centroids were computed from a snapshot of the data that no longer matches reality after enough edits, and nobody wants to re-run k-means clustering over the whole collection after every single delete.

This is the core tension every production vector database has to resolve: keep the index's read performance (the entire reason to use HNSW or IVF instead of brute force in the first place) while still supporting a write-heavy, edit-heavy real-world workload. The resolution nearly every system converges on is to *defer* the expensive structural work rather than do it synchronously per edit -- which is exactly what a tombstone is for.

sections.heading: Tombstones: Marking Instead of Removing
sections.body:
A **tombstone** is a marker recorded against a vector's ID saying 'this is deleted' without actually touching the underlying graph or cluster structure at all. The vector's coordinates typically stay exactly where they were -- still a node in the HNSW graph, still a member of its IVF cluster -- but a lookup table (or a bit in the vector's own stored record) flags it as deleted. Every query path checks this flag and filters tombstoned vectors out of the *results* it returns to the caller, even though the underlying traversal or cluster scan may still pass through -- or even land directly on -- the tombstoned node while searching.

That last detail is worth sitting with, because it's the part people find counterintuitive: a tombstoned vector keeps doing structural work for the index even after it's 'deleted.' In HNSW specifically, a tombstoned node often keeps serving as a waypoint other queries route through on their way to some other, still-live node -- removing it immediately would mean re-linking its neighbors right now, which is exactly the synchronous cost tombstoning is designed to avoid. The tradeoff is deliberate: a delete becomes an O(1) flag write instead of an O(graph-repair) structural edit, at the cost of that vector's storage and traversal overhead sticking around until some later cleanup pass actually reclaims it.

```python
class TombstoneIndex:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vectors = {}      # id -> vector (stays here even after "delete")
        self.deleted = set()   # tombstone markers

    def delete(self, vector_id):
        # O(1): flag it, don't touch the underlying structure at all
        self.deleted.add(vector_id)

    def search(self, query, k, distance_fn):
        scanned = 0
        results = []
        for vector_id, vec in self.vectors.items():
            scanned += 1                      # tombstoned nodes are still visited
            if vector_id in self.deleted:
                continue                       # ...but excluded from results
            results.append((vector_id, distance_fn(query, vec)))
        results.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[1])
        return results[:k], scanned
```

This toy index makes the mechanism explicit: `delete` never touches `self.vectors` at all, and `search` still iterates over every vector -- including tombstoned ones, which cost a real loop iteration and a real dict lookup -- before filtering them out of what it hands back. A real HNSW or IVF implementation is more sophisticated about *which* nodes it visits, but the shape of the tradeoff is identical: cheap delete now, deferred cleanup cost later.

sections.heading: Upsert Semantics: Insert-or-Update Keyed by a Stable ID
sections.body:
An **upsert** ('update or insert') is the operation almost every production vector database exposes as its primary write API: given a caller-supplied ID and a vector (plus optional metadata), either insert it as new if that ID has never been seen, or replace whatever was previously stored under that ID if it has. The entire mechanism depends on the ID being **stable** -- the same logical piece of content (the same document, the same chunk) must be upserted under the same ID every time it's re-embedded, or the system has no way to know it's looking at an update rather than a brand-new, unrelated item.

This matters more than it sounds, because it's exactly where a specific, common bug creeps in: a pipeline that re-processes a knowledge base periodically (say, nightly) and calls something like `insert(embed(doc))` without ever supplying a stable ID for `doc`, relying on the vector database to auto-generate a fresh ID for every insert. Every nightly run re-embeds and re-inserts *every* document as a brand-new entry, and the old entries from the previous run are never touched, let alone removed -- the collection silently grows without bound, accumulating stale duplicates of every document that was ever re-processed, all still fully live and fully searchable, competing with their own more current versions in every future query's results.

```python
def broken_reindex(documents, store, embed_fn):
    # BROKEN: uses list.append with an auto-incrementing id -- every run
    # creates brand new entries, never replacing the previous run's entries
    for doc in documents:
        new_id = len(store)
        store[new_id] = (embed_fn(doc["text"]), doc)

def correct_reindex(documents, store, embed_fn):
    # CORRECT: upsert keyed by the document's own stable id -- reprocessing
    # the same document overwrites its previous vector instead of duplicating it
    for doc in documents:
        store[doc["id"]] = (embed_fn(doc["text"]), doc)
```

A closely related distinction, and one worth internalizing separately: **not every update to a document requires re-embedding.** If only a document's metadata changes -- a permissions tag, a category label, a `last_reviewed` timestamp -- the vector itself, which encodes the *semantic content* of the document, hasn't changed at all, and a well-designed system lets you patch just the metadata fields cheaply, without touching the stored vector or its position in the index. But if the document's actual *text* changes -- a policy is edited, a paragraph is rewritten -- the old vector is now describing content that no longer exists at that ID; only a fresh call to the embedding model on the new text, followed by an upsert of the resulting vector under that same stable ID, keeps the index honest. Patching metadata is cheap and vector-shape-preserving; patching content silently, without re-embedding, leaves a vector in the index that's semantically lying about what's stored under its ID -- and nothing about the system will ever raise an error to tell you that happened.

sections.heading: Compaction and Reindexing: Paying Off Tombstone Debt
sections.body:
Tombstoning defers cost rather than eliminating it, and that deferred cost is real: every tombstoned vector still occupies memory, still gets visited during graph traversal or cluster scans, and in IVF's case, a growing pile of deleted-but-still-present vectors slowly pulls cluster centroids away from where the *actual, live* data is now concentrated -- the exact same 'stale centroids drift from the real data distribution' problem covered in the indexing-and-recall concept, just caused by deletions instead of new insertions. A collection that's had 40% of its original vectors tombstoned over time, but never compacted, is paying close to the full memory and traversal cost of the *original* 100%, while only 60% of that work has any chance of contributing a useful result to any query.

**Compaction** (sometimes called a rebuild, or a merge, depending on the system) is the periodic maintenance operation that actually pays off this debt: it walks the underlying structure, physically discards tombstoned vectors, and rebuilds (or repairs) whatever graph edges or cluster assignments depended on them -- reclaiming the memory and restoring the index to a state where its traversal cost reflects only the *live* data, not the live data plus however much dead weight has accumulated since the last cleanup.

```python
def compact(index):
    # Rebuild the live-only structure from scratch, discarding tombstones
    live_vectors = {
        vector_id: vec
        for vector_id, vec in index.vectors.items()
        if vector_id not in index.deleted
    }
    index.vectors = live_vectors
    index.deleted = set()   # nothing left to tombstone -- it's all been purged
    return index
```

The operational question compaction raises is *when*: it's not free to run (rebuilding a large HNSW graph is real, non-trivial compute), so mature systems schedule it periodically -- during low-traffic windows, or triggered once the tombstone ratio crosses some threshold (say, more than 15-20% of the collection) -- rather than continuously, and often perform it as a rolling, background rebuild that swaps in the compacted structure atomically once ready, so live queries keep working against the old structure until the new one is ready, with no downtime window at all. A common operational mistake is treating compaction as optional 'cleanup we'll get to eventually' rather than a load-bearing part of running a delete-heavy system: a multi-tenant product where tenants routinely delete and re-upload content, or a system honoring data-erasure requests, can accumulate tombstones fast enough that skipping compaction for too long turns into a real, user-visible latency regression -- one that looks, from a monitoring dashboard, exactly like 'the index is just getting slower for no reason,' when the actual reason is a specific, fixable maintenance task nobody scheduled.

examples.title: Tombstones Accumulate Real Cost Even Though Deletes Stay Cheap
examples.explanation: Deleting the 16 original documents only adds them to `deleted` -- it never shrinks `self.vectors` -- and the 5 new upserts add 5 more entries on top, so `self.vectors` ends up holding all 25 entries that were ever inserted (20 + 5), of which 16 are tombstoned. `search` loops over every one of those 25 entries before filtering, so `scanned_before` comes out as 25, even though only 9 documents (25 minus the 16 tombstoned) are actually live and could ever appear in a result. Calling `compact()` physically discards the 16 tombstoned entries, so `self.vectors` and `self.deleted` both settle at (9, 0), and `scanned_after` drops to 9 -- almost a 3x reduction in per-query traversal work, for the exact same set of live documents and the exact same query results. Nothing about the deletes or the new upserts was incorrect on its own; the waste comes purely from letting tombstones from a shrinking, actively-used collection pile up indefinitely without ever paying down that debt via compaction.

examples.title: Upsert-by-ID vs. ID-less Append: Duplicate Accumulation
examples.explanation: `broken_reindex` never uses the document's own stable `id` field at all -- it keys every entry by `len(store)`, a counter that only ever grows, so a second reprocessing run of the exact same single document creates a second, brand-new entry (`broken_store` ends up with 2 entries) instead of replacing the first. `correct_reindex` keys every entry by `doc["id"]`, so the second run's write lands on the exact same key as the first and overwrites it in place -- `correct_store` stays at exactly 1 entry no matter how many times the same document is reprocessed. At real scale, this is precisely the bug that lets a nightly reindex job quietly double, triple, and eventually multiply a collection's size run over run, with every stale duplicate remaining fully live and competing for ranking position against its own more current version.

examples.title: A Metadata Patch Is Not a Substitute for Re-Embedding Changed Content
examples.explanation: The first block changes `text` directly and patches `last_reviewed`, but never calls the embedding model -- so `vector` still holds the embedding of the original '1 vacation day' sentence even though `text` now says '2 vacation days'. Nothing raises an error here: the record is perfectly well-formed, has a vector, has text, has a timestamp -- it's just semantically inconsistent, and every future similarity search against this ID is comparing against a vector that describes content this document no longer contains. Only `update_content`, which calls `embed_fn` on the new text and overwrites `vector` as part of the same operation, actually keeps the two in sync. This is the concrete version of the metadata-patch-versus-content-update distinction: cheap fields (timestamps, tags, permissions) can be patched freely with no vector impact, but the moment the text itself changes, the vector has to be recomputed and re-upserted, or the index starts silently lying about what a given ID actually represents.

misconceptions.description: Deleting a vector from an index removes it immediately and completely, the same way DELETE FROM works against a row in a relational table.
misconceptions.clarification: Most production vector databases implement delete as a tombstone -- an O(1) flag marking the ID as deleted -- rather than an immediate structural removal, precisely because actually excising a node from an HNSW graph (or rebalancing an IVF cluster) requires repairing whatever other structure depended on it, which is too expensive to do synchronously on every single delete. The tombstoned vector typically keeps occupying memory and keeps being visited during traversal (just filtered out of returned results) until a later compaction or rebuild pass physically reclaims it. This is invisible from the API's perspective -- delete() returns success immediately either way -- but it has a real, observable consequence: a delete-heavy workload that never triggers compaction accumulates dead weight that keeps costing memory and query latency long after the data was 'deleted.'

misconceptions.description: Upserting new metadata for an existing ID and upserting a changed embedding vector for that ID are the same kind of operation, cost-wise and correctness-wise -- both just 'update the record.'
misconceptions.clarification: A metadata-only patch (permissions, tags, a timestamp) doesn't touch the vector at all -- the semantic content hasn't changed, so there's nothing to re-embed, and the update is cheap and doesn't affect the vector's position in the index's structure. A content change is fundamentally different: the old vector describes content that no longer exists at that ID, and the only way to keep the index honest is to re-run the embedding model on the new content and upsert the resulting vector under the same ID. Treating a content change as if it were a metadata patch -- editing the stored text without recomputing the vector -- produces a record that looks completely valid (it has a vector, it has text) but is semantically inconsistent, and nothing in the system raises an error to flag that mismatch; it just silently returns stale, wrong similarity scores for that document from then on.

exercises.prompt: This simulates five churn cycles (delete five, re-upsert five under new ids) against a 10-item index with no compaction, then calls compact(). What does it print, and why does the scanned count change the way it does?
hints: Each of the 3 cycles deletes 4 existing entries (tombstoning them, not removing them from self.vectors) and upserts 4 brand-new versioned entries -- so self.vectors only ever grows.
Count total entries in self.vectors after all 3 cycles: the original 10, plus 4 new versioned entries per cycle for 3 cycles.
search's scanned count reflects len(self.vectors) regardless of how many are tombstoned -- compact() is the only thing that actually shrinks it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: self.vectors starts with 10 entries (doc0..doc9). Each of the 3 cycles adds 4 brand-new versioned entries (doc0_v0..doc3_v0, then _v1, then _v2) without ever removing anything from self.vectors, so after 3 cycles it holds 10 + 4*3 = 22 entries -- scanned and len(self.vectors) both read 22. self.deleted, on the other hand, is a set, and every cycle deletes the exact same four literal ids -- doc0, doc1, doc2, doc3 -- again; re-adding an id that's already in a set doesn't grow it, so deleted stays fixed at exactly 4 unique ids throughout all 3 cycles, not 12. Calling compact() keeps only ids NOT in deleted: doc0 through doc3 (4 of the 22 entries) get discarded, dropping self.vectors to 22 - 4 = 18, and deleted resets to empty, giving the final (18, 18, 0). The key thing this exercise tests is the difference between what grows (self.vectors, via upserts of ever-new versioned ids) and what stays capped (self.deleted, since it only ever tracks 4 distinct original ids no matter how many times they're redundantly re-deleted) -- confusing 'deleted 4 times per cycle, 3 cycles' with 'deleted set size 12' is the natural mistake this is designed to catch.

exercises.prompt: A nightly job re-embeds a knowledge base and is supposed to keep the vector store's size equal to the number of source documents, no matter how many times it runs. Instead, the store's size doubles after every run. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Look at how entry_id is computed -- does it depend on anything about the document itself, or only on how many things are already in the store?
Every call to nightly_reindex with the SAME two documents should land on the SAME two keys in store, not two new ones -- what should the key actually be?
The documents already carry a stable identifier (doc['id']) that doesn't change between runs -- use that as the store's key instead of a counter.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is `entry_id = len(store)` -- it derives the key purely from how many entries already exist, with no connection to which document is being written. On the first run, store is empty, so faq-1 and faq-2 land at keys 0 and 1. On the second run, store already has 2 entries, so len(store) starts at 2, and the exact same two documents land at brand-new keys 2 and 3 instead of overwriting 0 and 1 -- doubling the store instead of refreshing it, and leaving the original two entries as stale, undeletable duplicates. The fix keys every entry by `doc["id"]`, the document's own stable identifier, which is identical across both runs for the same document -- so the second run's writes land on the exact same two keys as the first run and overwrite them in place, keeping the store's size at 2 no matter how many times the job runs. This is exactly the upsert-by-stable-id discipline every reindexing pipeline needs; a counter, a random id, or anything else that isn't tied to the document's own identity will eventually reproduce this same duplication bug.

assessments.prompt: Why do production vector databases typically mark a deleted vector with a tombstone rather than immediately excising it from the underlying HNSW graph or IVF cluster?
options: Tombstones are required because vector databases cannot physically delete data for legal/compliance reasons.

Immediately removing a node can require repairing the graph edges or cluster assignments that depended on it, which is too expensive to do synchronously on every single delete; tombstoning defers that cost to periodic compaction.
HNSW and IVF do not support deletion at all, so tombstoning is a workaround bolted on entirely outside the index.
Tombstoning is purely a caching optimization with no relationship to the graph or cluster structure itself.
assessments.explanation: A node in an HNSW graph often serves as a bridge that other nodes' navigability depends on, and a vector in an IVF cluster contributes to that cluster's effective structure -- removing either one correctly means repairing whatever depended on it, which is real, non-trivial work. Tombstoning turns a delete into an O(1) flag write, deferring the expensive structural repair to a periodic compaction pass instead of paying it synchronously on every delete call. Option A is wrong -- compliance requirements, if anything, push toward eventually purging data via compaction, not toward tombstoning as a legal workaround. Option C is wrong -- both structures do support deletion, just not as a free operation. Option D understates it -- tombstoning isn't just a caching layer, it's a real, deliberate deferral of structural index maintenance.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: 'I don't need to call the embedding model again -- I'll just update the document's text field directly in the vector store and it'll be up to date.' Explain what's wrong with this plan and what actually happens if it ships this way.
assessments.modelAnswer: The vector stored alongside a document is a numeric summary of that document's semantic content, produced by running the embedding model over the text at the time it was last embedded -- it is not automatically kept in sync with whatever the text field happens to say right now. If the teammate edits the text field directly without re-running the embedding model and re-upserting the resulting vector, the record ends up in an inconsistent state: `text` says one thing, but `vector` still encodes whatever the *previous* text said, because nothing about editing a text field triggers re-embedding on its own. Critically, nothing in the system raises an error or warning for this -- the record is perfectly well-formed (a valid vector, valid text, valid metadata), so it passes every structural check a database might run. What actually happens downstream is silent and hard to diagnose: every future similarity search that matches against this document's vector is being scored against the *old* content, not the new content the user can currently see -- a query that should now match the updated text might not surface this document at all, while a query that matches the old, no-longer-true text might surface it when it shouldn't. The fix is to treat any content change as requiring the same two-step upsert every fresh insert would need: re-embed the new text through the model, then upsert the resulting vector under the document's existing, stable ID, so the vector and the text it's supposed to represent stay in lockstep. Metadata-only fields (tags, permissions, a review timestamp) are the one case where a direct patch really is safe and doesn't need re-embedding, precisely because they don't change what the document's content actually says.

concepts.title: Metadata Filtering at Scale: Pre-Filter vs. Post-Filter Tradeoffs
concepts.description: Choosing between pre-filtering and post-filtering isn't a one-time architectural choice you make and forget -- filter selectivity is a number that changes as your data and your query patterns change, and a fixed oversampling factor tuned for one filter in isolation can silently start failing the moment a second filter gets ANDed on top of it.
learningObjectives: Derive an approximate cost model relating desired result count k, filter selectivity, and the overfetch factor needed for post-filtering to reliably return k results.
Implement and trace the 'oversample and re-rank' (adaptive expansion) pattern for post-filtering against a low-selectivity filter.

Explain how ANDing multiple simultaneous filters (tenant scope, soft-delete exclusion, recency window) compounds their selectivities, and why a factor tuned for one filter alone can fail once combined with others.
Explain why filter selectivity drifts over time as a live property of the data, not a fixed constant, and why a filtering strategy needs periodic re-validation.
Decide, given a filter's approximate selectivity and cardinality, whether naive pre-filtering, post-filtering with oversampling, or a dedicated partition is the more appropriate strategy.

sections.heading: Recap and Reframe: Selectivity Is the Variable That Decides
sections.body:
The metadata filtering concept earlier in this subject established the two baseline strategies -- post-filtering (search first, filter the results afterward) can silently return fewer than k results even when plenty of matching data exists elsewhere in the collection, while pre-filtering (filter first, search only the matching subset) is correct by construction but typically means scanning that filtered subset directly, bypassing whatever ANN speedup the underlying index would otherwise provide. At small scale, or with a highly selective filter, that bypass is a non-issue -- scanning a few hundred filtered candidates directly is fast regardless of whether an ANN index is involved at all. The entire question this concept exists to answer is: at what point does that stop being true, and what do you actually do about it?

The answer is quantitative, not a rule of thumb: it depends on the filter's **selectivity** -- the fraction of the collection that satisfies it. A tenant filter that matches 0.05% of a huge multi-tenant collection (a small customer among thousands) is a completely different situation from a boolean flag that matches 60% of the collection; the first is exactly where naive pre-filtering shines (scan a tiny, cheap subset directly), and the second is exactly where naive pre-filtering degenerates back toward scanning most of the index by hand, having thrown away the reason you built an ANN index over it. Framing the decision around a measurable number -- selectivity -- rather than a fixed rule ('always pre-filter,' 'always post-filter') is what actually lets you reason about a specific filter on a specific collection, rather than applying advice that was true for someone else's very different data shape.

sections.heading: A Cost Model for Post-Filtering: How Much Do You Actually Need to Overfetch?
sections.body:
Post-filtering's core failure mode -- silently returning fewer than k results -- has a fix that's almost embarrassingly simple once you frame it in terms of selectivity: **ask the ANN index for more than k results, filter afterward, and ask for enough more that you can expect at least k of them to survive the filter.** If a filter's selectivity is `s` (a fraction between 0 and 1), and you fetch `n` unfiltered candidates from the ANN index, the number you'd expect to pass the filter is roughly `n * s` (assuming the filter's matches are distributed roughly evenly through the ranking, which is a simplifying assumption worth flagging up front -- real data isn't always that uniform, but it's a reasonable starting point for sizing the overfetch). Solving for the `n` that makes `n * s >= k` gives a simple, useful approximation:

```python
import math

def required_overfetch(k, selectivity):
    return math.ceil(k / selectivity)

print(required_overfetch(10, 0.5))     # 20    -- a common condition, mild overfetch
print(required_overfetch(10, 0.05))    # 200   -- a fairly rare condition, real overfetch
print(required_overfetch(10, 0.001))   # 10000 -- a rare tenant, overfetch is now huge
```

That last line is the important warning sign: as selectivity keeps shrinking, the required overfetch keeps growing, and at some point 'fetch more unfiltered candidates from the ANN index' stops being meaningfully cheaper than 'just pre-filter and scan the matching subset directly' -- you're back to the same crossover point the previous section described, just approached from the other direction. This cost model is exactly what makes the pre-filter-vs-post-filter decision measurable instead of a guess: compute (or estimate from historical data) a filter's selectivity, plug it into this formula, and compare the resulting overfetch against what pre-filtering the same subset directly would cost.

sections.heading: Oversampling in Practice: Adaptive Expansion, Not a Fixed Guess
sections.body:
A single fixed overfetch factor, computed once from a selectivity estimate and hardcoded, is a reasonable starting point but a fragile production strategy -- selectivity estimates are approximations, and real data doesn't distribute filter matches perfectly evenly through the ranking the way the cost model assumes. The more robust pattern, used by real production retrieval systems, is **adaptive expansion**: start with a moderate overfetch, check whether it produced enough matching results, and if not, widen the net and try again, rather than betting everything on getting the overfetch factor exactly right on the first attempt.

```python
def adaptive_post_filter_search(query, documents, tenant, k, dist_fn, growth=4, max_candidates=None):
    if max_candidates is None:
        max_candidates = len(documents)
    n = k
    while True:
        candidates = sorted(documents, key=lambda name: dist_fn(query, documents[name][0]))[:n]
        matched = [name for name in candidates if documents[name][1] == tenant]
        if len(matched) >= k or n >= max_candidates:
            return matched[:k], n
        n = min(n * growth, max_candidates)   # widen the net and retry
```

Each retry costs additional latency -- another ANN query at a larger `n` -- so this pattern trades a small amount of worst-case latency (for the rare, low-selectivity queries that actually need several rounds of widening) for correctness on every query, rather than either accepting silent under-returns (naive post-filtering) or always paying pre-filtering's full-subset-scan cost even for filters that turn out to be more selective than expected. A capped `max_candidates` matters here for a subtle reason: without a ceiling, an extremely rare filter combined with a small collection could spiral toward re-fetching the entire index on every retry, which defeats the entire purpose of oversampling in the first place -- the cap is what turns 'try progressively harder' into 'try progressively harder, and then fall back to whatever partial result you have, rather than degrading into a full scan disguised as a retry loop.'

sections.heading: Compounding Filters: Selectivity Multiplies, Not Adds
sections.body:
Real production queries are almost never governed by a single filter condition. A typical request scopes results to the requesting tenant, excludes soft-deleted (tombstoned) content, and often restricts to some recency window -- three separate `AND`-ed conditions layered on top of the raw similarity search. The critical arithmetic fact to internalize is that **independent filter conditions combined with AND multiply their selectivities together**, not add them: if the tenant filter alone matches 5% of the collection, the 'not soft-deleted' filter alone matches 90%, and the recency filter alone matches 30%, the combined selectivity of all three together is approximately `0.05 * 0.9 * 0.3 = 0.0135` -- roughly 1.35%, meaningfully lower than any single filter's own selectivity.

```python
import math

def required_overfetch(k, selectivity):
    return math.ceil(k / selectivity)

tenant_selectivity = 0.05
not_deleted_selectivity = 0.9
recency_selectivity = 0.3
combined_selectivity = tenant_selectivity * not_deleted_selectivity * recency_selectivity

print(round(combined_selectivity, 4))                       # 0.0135
print(required_overfetch(10, tenant_selectivity))            # 200  -- tuned for tenant filter alone
print(required_overfetch(10, combined_selectivity))          # 741  -- what's actually needed now
```

This is exactly the trap a real team falls into: an oversampling factor of 200 gets tuned and validated against the tenant filter early in a product's life, ships, and works fine -- until a 'not soft-deleted' exclusion and a recency window get added later, each individually reasonable, each individually tested. No single change looks dangerous, but the combined effect quietly drops the true required overfetch from 200 to over 700, and the team's still-hardcoded factor of 200 starts silently under-returning results for a meaningful fraction of queries, with nothing in the system raising an alarm -- it just looks like search 'sometimes returns fewer results than expected,' which is easy to dismiss as noise until someone does the arithmetic.

sections.heading: Selectivity Drift: The Same Number Doesn't Stay the Same
sections.body:
Everything in this concept treats selectivity as a number you can plug into a formula, but it's worth being explicit that this number is a live property of your *current* data, not a fixed constant baked into a filter's definition. A tenant's document count grows over time relative to the rest of the collection; a recency window's selectivity mechanically shifts as the wall clock moves forward and the boundary of 'the last 30 days' slides across a stream of continuously-arriving content; a new feature might introduce a new common value for a filter field that changes its overall distribution. An oversampling factor -- fixed or adaptively-capped -- that was correctly sized against last quarter's selectivity can quietly become undersized as the underlying selectivity drifts, exactly the same 'stale tuning' risk already covered for ANN recall parameters like `nprobe` and `ef_search` earlier in this subject, just applied to filter selectivity instead of index recall.

The practical mitigation is monitoring, not a one-time calculation: log how often post-filter or adaptive-expansion queries actually hit their `max_candidates` ceiling without reaching k results (a direct, measurable shortfall signal), and periodically re-estimate selectivity for your most common filter combinations against current data, the same way index recall gets re-validated after a model or data-distribution change. Treating a filtering strategy as something you configure once at launch and never revisit is precisely how a system that worked correctly on day one quietly degrades into one that silently returns incomplete results months later, with no code change and no error anywhere to point at.

examples.title: Sizing the Overfetch: Why a Rare Filter Needs a Much Bigger Net
examples.explanation: required_overfetch answers 'how many unfiltered candidates do I need to fetch so that, on average, at least k of them survive a filter with this selectivity?' At selectivity 0.5 (a common condition, like 'not soft-deleted' in a lightly-churned collection), fetching 20 candidates for k=10 is a mild, cheap overfetch. At selectivity 0.05 (a modest-sized tenant among many), the same k=10 now needs 200 unfiltered candidates -- a real, non-trivial widening of the ANN query. At selectivity 0.001 (a genuinely rare condition -- a small tenant in a huge shared collection), the required overfetch balloons to 10,000, at which point fetching that many unfiltered candidates from the ANN index may cost more than just pre-filtering the matching subset directly and scanning it by hand. The formula doesn't tell you which strategy to pick -- it tells you the actual cost of committing to post-filtering for a given selectivity, which is exactly the number you need before you can compare it against pre-filtering's cost for the same filter.

examples.title: Adaptive Expansion: Widening the Net Until Enough Results Survive
examples.explanation: tenant_small owns exactly 5 of the 50 documents (every 10th one: doc0, doc10, doc20, doc30, doc40), ranked at positions 1, 11, 21, 31, 41 in the unfiltered distance ordering. The first attempt fetches only n=2 unfiltered candidates (doc0, doc1) and finds 1 match (doc0) -- not enough for k=2, so it widens to n=6, still only finding doc0 (doc10 is ranked 11th, still outside the top 6). Widening again to n=18 finally brings doc10 (ranked 11th) into view, giving 2 matches -- which meets k=2, so the loop stops there, returning ['doc0', 'doc10'] after ultimately fetching 18 unfiltered candidates. Notice the loop didn't need to guess the right overfetch up front; it started conservatively and only paid for wider fetches on the attempts that actually needed them, which is exactly the robustness advantage adaptive expansion has over committing to one fixed overfetch factor and hoping it's enough.

examples.title: Compounding Filters Silently Break a Factor Tuned for Only One
examples.code:
import math

def required_overfetch(k, selectivity):
    return math.ceil(k / selectivity)

tenant_selectivity = 0.05
not_deleted_selectivity = 0.9
recency_selectivity = 0.3
combined_selectivity = tenant_selectivity * not_deleted_selectivity * recency_selectivity

print(round(combined_selectivity, 4))
print(required_overfetch(10, tenant_selectivity))
print(required_overfetch(10, combined_selectivity))
examples.explanation: When only the tenant filter was in play, selectivity was 0.05 and a k=10 query needed 200 unfiltered candidates -- a factor a team might reasonably measure once and hardcode. Multiplying in the two later-added filters (not-deleted at 0.9, recency at 0.3) drops the combined selectivity to 0.0135, because AND-ing independent filters multiplies their selectivities rather than averaging or adding them -- the combined condition is meaningfully rarer than any single one of its parts. The true required overfetch for the same k=10 jumps from 200 to 741, more than 3.5x higher, even though neither the not-deleted filter nor the recency filter looks even remotely as narrow as the tenant filter on its own. A team that hardcoded 200 based on the tenant filter alone, and never re-measured after adding the other two filters, is now silently under-fetching on a large share of its queries -- exactly the kind of regression that has no error message and no obvious trigger, because every individual filter addition looked perfectly safe in isolation.

misconceptions.description: Since pre-filtering guarantees correctness (it never misses matching results the way naive post-filtering can), you should always pre-filter, and post-filtering has no place in a well-built production system.
misconceptions.clarification: Pre-filtering's correctness comes with a real cost: it typically means scanning the filtered subset directly, bypassing whatever ANN speedup (HNSW's graph, IVF's clusters) the index would otherwise provide over the full collection. That's cheap and clearly the right call when the filter is highly selective -- a small subset relative to the whole collection. But for a low-selectivity filter that matches a large share of the collection, naive pre-filtering degenerates toward scanning most of the index by hand, which defeats the entire point of having built an ANN index in the first place. Post-filtering with proper oversampling (or adaptive expansion) is often the better-performing, still-correct choice for exactly those high-selectivity-in-the-other-direction cases -- the right strategy is a function of the specific filter's selectivity, not a blanket rule that one approach is always safer.

misconceptions.description: An oversampling factor for post-filtering that reliably returns k results in testing is safe to hardcode permanently, since it's a fixed property of how much bigger you need to fetch.
misconceptions.clarification: The required overfetch factor is entirely a function of the filter's current selectivity, and selectivity is not a fixed constant -- it drifts as a tenant's data grows relative to the rest of the collection, as a recency window's boundary mechanically slides forward over time, and it multiplies down sharply the moment a new filter condition gets ANDed on top of an existing one, even if that new filter looks individually harmless. A factor validated once against a single filter, or against an early data distribution, can silently become undersized later with no code change and no error -- the fix is treating selectivity as something to monitor and periodically re-measure, the same discipline already required for ANN recall parameters like nprobe and ef_search, rather than a value you compute once at launch and never revisit.

exercises.prompt: Given a 50-document collection where every 10th document belongs to 'tenant_small' and the rest belong to 'tenant_big', what does this adaptive post-filter search print, and how many widening attempts does it take?
hints: tenant_small's documents are doc0, doc10, doc20, doc30, doc40 -- ranked at positions 1, 11, 21, 31, and 41 in the unfiltered distance ordering (closest to farthest from query (0.0, 0.0)).
Trace n through the loop: it starts at k=2, and each failed attempt multiplies n by growth=3 (2, then 6, then 18, ...) until enough matches are found or n reaches max_candidates.
At each n, count how many of tenant_small's five ranked positions (1, 11, 21, 31, 41) fall within the top n -- that's how many matches that attempt finds.
exercises.solutionExplanation: At n=2, the top 2 unfiltered candidates are doc0 and doc1 -- only doc0 belongs to tenant_small, so matched has 1 entry, short of k=2, and the trace records (2, 1). Widening to n=6 (2*3) still only includes doc0 among tenant_small's documents, since doc10 is ranked 11th, outside the top 6 -- trace records (6, 1), still short. Widening again to n=18 (6*3) now includes ranks 1 through 18, which covers both doc0 (rank 1) and doc10 (rank 11) -- 2 matches, meeting k=2, so the loop stops and records (18, 2). The final result is ['doc0', 'doc10'] with n_used=18, reached after two failed widening attempts and one successful one. This is exactly the adaptive-expansion pattern working as intended: it never had to know in advance that n=18 would be the right size, it just kept trying progressively wider fetches until one actually worked.

Then write `combined_selectivity(*selectivities)` that multiplies any number of independent filter selectivities together. Use both to check whether a team's hardcoded overfetch of 150 (tuned for a single 0.08-selectivity tenant filter) is still enough once a 0.6-selectivity 'not deleted' filter is ANDed on top, for k=15.

exercises.solutionCode:
import math

def required_overfetch(k, selectivity):
    return math.ceil(k / selectivity)


def combined_selectivity(*selectivities):
    result = 1.0
    for s in selectivities:
        result *= s
    return result


hardcoded_overfetch = 150
k = 15
tenant_selectivity = 0.08
not_deleted_selectivity = 0.6

single_filter_requirement = required_overfetch(k, tenant_selectivity)
combined = combined_selectivity(tenant_selectivity, not_deleted_selectivity)
combined_requirement = required_overfetch(k, combined)

print(single_filter_requirement)
print(round(combined, 4))
print(combined_requirement)
print(hardcoded_overfetch >= combined_requirement)
exercises.solutionExplanation: required_overfetch(15, 0.08) comes out to 188 (math.ceil(15 / 0.08) = math.ceil(187.5) = 188) -- already more than the hardcoded 150, meaning the tenant filter alone was already slightly under-provisioned by this exact model, but combined_selectivity(0.08, 0.6) = 0.048 makes it dramatically worse: required_overfetch(15, 0.048) = math.ceil(312.5) = 313. hardcoded_overfetch (150) >= combined_requirement (313) is False -- the team's fixed factor is now covering less than half of what's actually needed once the second filter is ANDed on, exactly the silent-shortfall scenario this concept warns about. Note that this exercise's numbers were chosen so that even the single-filter requirement (188) already exceeds the hardcoded value (150) -- a reminder that 'it happened to work in testing' isn't the same as 'it was correctly sized,' since a team might get lucky in a small test environment even when the underlying math already didn't support their chosen factor.

assessments.prompt: A team tuned their post-filter oversampling factor against their tenant_id filter alone, and it reliably returned enough results for months. After adding a mandatory 'not soft-deleted' filter and a recency window on top of the existing tenant filter, the same fixed oversampling factor starts silently returning fewer than k results for many queries. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The ANN index became corrupted when the new filter conditions were added.

Combining multiple independent filters with AND multiplies their selectivities together, so the effective selectivity of tenant AND not-deleted AND recency is substantially lower than the tenant filter's selectivity alone -- the old factor was sized for a selectivity that no longer applies.
Post-filtering fundamentally cannot support more than one filter condition at a time.
The recency filter should have replaced the similarity search entirely rather than being combined with it.
assessments.explanation: Selectivities multiply, not add, when independent filter conditions are ANDed together -- a tenant filter that matches 5% of the collection combined with a not-deleted filter matching 90% and a recency filter matching 30% yields a combined selectivity around 1.35%, meaningfully rarer than the tenant filter was on its own. An oversampling factor sized correctly for the tenant filter alone is very likely undersized for that much lower combined selectivity, which produces exactly the observed symptom: queries that used to reliably return k results now sometimes fall short, with no error anywhere to flag it. Option A is a fabricated failure mode unrelated to how filtering actually works. Option C is wrong -- post-filtering handles any number of ANDed conditions fine, it's the sizing of the overfetch that needs to account for their combined effect. Option D is a non-sequitur -- recency being a filter condition doesn't mean it should replace similarity search; it's meant to be combined with it, which is exactly what's happening here.

assessments.prompt: A teammate proposes: 'Pre-filtering is always correct and post-filtering can silently under-return -- let's just always pre-filter everywhere and never worry about this again.' Explain why this isn't automatically the right call at scale, referencing selectivity and how ANN indexes work.
assessments.modelAnswer: Pre-filtering really is correct by construction -- restricting to the matching subset before ranking guarantees you never miss a matching result the way naive post-filtering can. But 'correct' and 'fast' are separate properties, and pre-filtering's speed depends entirely on how selective the filter actually is. HNSW's graph and IVF's clusters are built once, over the entire collection, specifically to make nearest-neighbor search over that whole collection fast; naive pre-filtering, as usually implemented, restricts to the matching subset and then computes distances directly against every member of that subset, which isn't using the ANN index's structure at all for the filtered search -- it's a plain scan, just over a smaller set than the full collection. For a highly selective filter (a small tenant among many, say), that smaller set really is small, and scanning it directly is fast regardless of ANN structure. But for a filter that matches a large fraction of the collection -- a boolean flag true for 70% of documents, say -- 'the matching subset' is nearly the whole collection, and pre-filtering degenerates into something close to a full brute-force scan, precisely the cost the ANN index was built to avoid in the first place. So 'always pre-filter' trades away a real, measurable performance benefit (the ANN index's speedup) specifically in the cases where the filter doesn't narrow things down much -- which are common in practice (soft-delete exclusions, broad category filters). The better approach is to actually estimate or measure the filter's selectivity and choose per-filter: pre-filter when selective, use post-filtering with proper oversampling (fixed or adaptive) when not, or fall back to a dedicated partition/namespace strategy for filters that are both broad and extremely frequent -- not commit to one strategy unconditionally for every filter a system will ever see.

concepts.title: Namespace and Partition Strategies for Multi-Tenant Data
concepts.description: A tenant_id metadata filter on a shared index and a dedicated namespace per tenant look interchangeable on paper -- both scope search results to one customer's data -- but they make opposite tradeoffs between per-tenant overhead, blast radius when something goes wrong, and how cleanly a tenant's data can be fully erased, and picking the wrong default for your tenant size distribution has real operational cost.
learningObjectives: Compare shared-index-with-metadata-filter, namespace-per-tenant, and hashed-partition strategies for multi-tenant vector storage, and state the primary tradeoff each one makes.
Explain the 'noisy neighbor' problem in a shared vector index and why physical namespace separation mitigates it.
Explain why per-namespace baseline overhead makes namespace-per-tenant scale poorly for a large number of small tenants, and describe a hybrid/tiered strategy that addresses that.
Connect data-erasure requirements (such as GDPR's 'right to be forgotten') to the choice between relying on tombstoned metadata filters and physically separate, droppable namespaces.
Identify tenant size skew as a partitioning risk and describe dedicating separate namespaces to outlier 'whale' tenants as a mitigation.

sections.heading: Three Shapes for Multi-Tenant Storage
sections.body:
Every strategy for storing multiple tenants' vectors ultimately picks a point on the same spectrum: how much physical separation exists between one tenant's data and another's. Three shapes show up constantly in practice.

**Shared index with a metadata filter** is the approach the previous two concepts already assumed: every tenant's vectors live in the same underlying HNSW graph or IVF clusters, and a `tenant_id` field in each vector's metadata is filtered on at query time (via pre-filtering, post-filtering, or filtered graph traversal) to scope results to the requesting tenant. It's the simplest to operate -- one index to build, tune, and monitor -- and it amortizes the index's fixed structural overhead across every tenant at once.

**Namespace-per-tenant** (sometimes called a collection-per-tenant, or a class-per-tenant depending on the specific vector database's terminology) gives each tenant their own physically separate index structure -- its own HNSW graph, its own IVF clusters, entirely independent of every other tenant's. No metadata filter is needed at query time at all, because there's nothing to filter: a query against tenant A's namespace can only ever see tenant A's vectors, by construction, not by a runtime check.

**Hashed/sharded partitioning** sits between the two: tenants are routed, typically via a hash of their tenant ID, into one of a fixed, moderate number of physical partitions (shards), each of which holds many different tenants' data together (still requiring a metadata filter within a shard) but far fewer than the full collection. This trades away namespace-per-tenant's complete isolation for a bounded number of physical structures, rather than one per tenant or one for everybody.

sections.heading: The Noisy Neighbor Problem and Blast Radius
sections.body:
A shared index means shared resources: the same CPU threads walking the same HNSW graph, the same disk I/O reading the same underlying segment files, the same write throughput budget for upserts and deletes, all divided across every tenant using that index at any given moment. If one tenant issues a sudden burst of traffic -- a bulk reindex, a viral spike in end-user queries -- every other tenant sharing that same index competes for the exact same underlying resources during that burst, and their query latency degrades right along with it, even though their own usage pattern hasn't changed at all. This is the **noisy neighbor problem**, and it's a direct, mechanical consequence of physical sharing, not a bug in any particular implementation.

```python
def simulate_shared_queue(capacity_per_tick, tenant_a_burst, tenant_b_requests_per_tick, ticks):
    queue = []
    wait_times = []
    for t in range(ticks):
        if t == 0:
            queue.extend([("A", t)] * tenant_a_burst)
        queue.extend([("B", t)] * tenant_b_requests_per_tick)
        served = queue[:capacity_per_tick]
        queue = queue[capacity_per_tick:]
        for tenant, arrival_tick in served:
            if tenant == "B":
                wait_times.append(t - arrival_tick)
    return wait_times

shared_waits = simulate_shared_queue(capacity_per_tick=10, tenant_a_burst=90, tenant_b_requests_per_tick=1, ticks=15)
print(shared_waits)
print(round(sum(shared_waits) / len(shared_waits), 2))
```

A second, entirely separate risk shares the same root cause: **blast radius**. If a filtering bug -- a missing WHERE-clause-equivalent, a bypassed permission check -- ever slips into a shared index, the potential damage is bounded only by however many tenants share that one index, which in a large shared deployment could mean every single customer's data is theoretically exposed by one bug in one code path. A dedicated namespace per tenant doesn't make bugs impossible, but it does bound the damage of any single bug to the one tenant whose namespace it occurred in -- a fundamentally smaller blast radius, achieved through physical separation rather than runtime correctness, which is exactly the kind of defense-in-depth property that's valuable specifically *because* it doesn't rely on every single filter check being bug-free forever.

sections.heading: Why Namespace-Per-Tenant Doesn't Scale Unboundedly
Erasure, Compliance, and Choosing a Default
sections.body:
Regulations like GDPR's 'right to erasure' create a concrete, legally-binding forcing function for this whole decision: when a tenant (or an end user whose data a tenant stores) demands their data be deleted, the system needs to actually, verifiably remove it -- not just hide it. In a shared index relying on metadata filters and tombstones, 'deleting' a tenant's data means tombstoning every one of their vectors and then waiting for (or explicitly triggering) a compaction pass to physically purge them -- correct, but with a real gap in between where the tombstoned-but-not-yet-purged data still physically exists, still occupies storage, and depends on the same compaction discipline covered earlier in this module actually running reliably and promptly. A namespace-per-tenant deployment has a structurally simpler answer: dropping the entire namespace is a single, atomic, immediately-verifiable operation -- there's no in-between state where the data lingers, tombstoned, waiting for a background job.

Putting the whole decision together, a reasonable default framework looks like this: start with a shared index plus metadata filtering for the common case of many small-to-medium tenants, where per-namespace overhead would dominate and a single well-tested filtering and compaction pipeline is easier to operate correctly than thousands of independent ones. Introduce hashed partitioning once query volume or noisy-neighbor incidents on the shared index become a real operational problem, to bound the blast radius and resource contention to a fixed number of shards rather than the whole tenant population. Reserve dedicated namespaces specifically for tenants whose size makes the per-namespace overhead negligible, whose compliance requirements demand the strongest, simplest erasure guarantee available, or both -- rather than treating 'give everyone their own namespace' or 'put everyone in one shared index' as a single, permanent, one-size-fits-all answer.

examples.title: Per-Namespace Overhead Compounds With Tenant Count -- and Disappears for a Whale
examples.explanation: At 100 tenants averaging 200 vectors each, namespace-per-tenant's total footprint (about 0.24 GB) comes out roughly 4.12x larger than a shared index holding the identical data (about 0.06 GB), purely because the 2MB baseline overhead gets paid 100 times instead of once. At 10,000 tenants, that ratio has grown to about 4.25x -- the gap widens as tenant count grows, because the per-tenant overhead scales with num_tenants while the shared index's overhead stays flat. The final two lines show why the same fixed overhead behaves completely differently depending on tenant size: for a 50-million-vector whale, the 2MB baseline is about 0.0013% of that tenant's own footprint -- effectively free -- while for a 200-vector tenant, that identical 2MB overhead is about 76.5% of the total footprint, meaning three-quarters of the storage 'cost' of giving that tenant their own namespace is pure fixed overhead, not their actual data. This is the numeric case for pooling small tenants and reserving dedicated namespaces for whales, not a rule of thumb.

examples.title: Noisy Neighbor: One Tenant's Burst Delays Another Tenant's Ordinary Traffic
examples.code:
def simulate_shared_queue(capacity_per_tick, tenant_a_burst, tenant_b_requests_per_tick, ticks):
    queue = []
    wait_times = []
    for t in range(ticks):
        if t == 0:
            queue.extend([("A", t)] * tenant_a_burst)
        queue.extend([("B", t)] * tenant_b_requests_per_tick)
        served = queue[:capacity_per_tick]
        queue = queue[capacity_per_tick:]
        for tenant, arrival_tick in served:
            if tenant == "B":
                wait_times.append(t - arrival_tick)
    return wait_times


shared_waits = simulate_shared_queue(capacity_per_tick=10, tenant_a_burst=90, tenant_b_requests_per_tick=1, ticks=15)
dedicated_waits = simulate_shared_queue(capacity_per_tick=10, tenant_a_burst=0, tenant_b_requests_per_tick=1, ticks=15)

print(shared_waits, round(sum(shared_waits) / len(shared_waits), 2))
print(dedicated_waits, round(sum(dedicated_waits) / len(dedicated_waits), 2))
examples.explanation: Tenant A dumps a 90-request burst into the shared queue at tick 0, arriving just before tenant B's steady trickle of 1 request per tick -- since A's requests were queued first, the fixed capacity of 10 requests per tick spends its first nine ticks working through A's backlog before B's very first request even gets served, at tick 9 (a wait of 9 ticks for a request that arrived at tick 0). Later requests from B wait progressively less as A's backlog drains, giving an average wait of 3.0 ticks across B's 15 requests. Rerunning the identical simulation with tenant_a_burst=0 -- modeling what B would experience with its own dedicated capacity, entirely unaffected by A's usage -- drops every one of B's wait times to 0. Nothing about tenant B's own request pattern changed between the two runs; the only difference is whether B's requests have to share a queue with tenant A's burst at all, which is exactly the noisy-neighbor effect a dedicated namespace (or a dedicated partition) is designed to eliminate.

examples.title: A Hybrid Router: Pool Small Tenants, Dedicate Namespaces to Whales
examples.explanation: route_tenant checks each tenant's vector count against a whale_threshold (1 million vectors here) before deciding where its data lives: tenant_whale, at 60 million vectors, clears that threshold and gets routed to its own dedicated_namespace, isolated from every other tenant's traffic and storage entirely. The three small tenants (300, 150, and 900 vectors -- all comfortably below the threshold) instead get hashed into one of 8 shared partitions via deterministic_hash(tenant_id) % 8, landing in shared_partition_2, shared_partition_3, and shared_partition_4 respectively -- pooled together with whatever other small tenants land in those same partitions, sharing the fixed per-partition overhead across many tenants instead of each paying it alone. This single routing function is the mechanical core of the hybrid strategy: no manual, one-off decision is needed per tenant, and a tenant that grows past the whale threshold over time can be migrated to its own dedicated namespace exactly when the overhead math actually justifies it, not before.

misconceptions.description: Using a tenant_id metadata filter on a shared index provides the same data-isolation guarantee as physically separate namespaces or collections -- both scope results to one tenant, so they're equally safe.
misconceptions.clarification: A metadata filter is a runtime check that depends on every single query path correctly applying it, every time, with no exceptions -- a missing filter clause, a caching layer that forgets to re-apply it, or a new code path that skips it can leak another tenant's data, and the potential blast radius of that single bug is bounded only by how many tenants share that index (in a large deployment, potentially all of them). A dedicated namespace provides isolation structurally: a query against tenant A's namespace has no path to tenant B's data at all, regardless of what any particular query's filtering logic does or fails to do. Both approaches can be implemented correctly, but they fail differently -- a filter bug in a shared index is a single point of failure for every tenant sharing it, while a bug affecting one dedicated namespace stays contained to that one tenant.

misconceptions.description: Giving every tenant, no matter how small, their own dedicated namespace or collection is the safest default, and it scales fine as the number of tenants grows.
misconceptions.clarification: Every dedicated namespace carries a fixed baseline overhead -- bookkeeping and graph/cluster structure that exists independent of how many vectors that namespace actually holds -- and that overhead gets paid once per namespace, not once total. For a large tenant, that fixed cost is negligible next to their actual data. For a large *population* of small tenants, the same fixed cost gets multiplied by the tenant count and can end up dominating the total storage footprint, sometimes representing the large majority of the cost for a genuinely small tenant, while a shared index pays that overhead exactly once regardless of tenant count. 'Safest' in the isolation sense and 'most efficient' in the resource sense are different axes, and namespace-per-tenant as a universal default optimizes only for the first at a real, compounding cost on the second -- which is exactly why production systems tend toward hybrid strategies instead of applying one policy to every tenant regardless of size.

exercises.prompt: For 500 tenants averaging 150 vectors each, what does this print, and what does the ratio tell you about namespace-per-tenant overhead at this tenant count?
hints: namespace_per_tenant_total pays baseline_overhead_bytes once PER tenant (500 times); shared_index_total pays it exactly once total -- both add the same total vector byte count (500 * 150 * 3072) on top.
Compute the vector-only bytes first: 500 * 150 * 3072. Then add 500 * 2,000,000 for the namespace version, or just 2,000,000 for the shared version.
gb() just converts bytes to gigabytes for readability -- the interesting number is the final ratio, n / s.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The shared vector byte count is the same in both formulas: 500 * 150 * 3072 = 230,400,000 bytes. namespace_per_tenant_total adds 500 * 2,000,000 = 1,000,000,000 bytes of baseline overhead on top, for a total of 1,230,400,000 bytes (about 1.1459 GB). shared_index_total adds only 2,000,000 bytes of baseline overhead (paid once), for a total of 232,400,000 bytes (about 0.2164 GB). The ratio, about 5.29, means giving these 500 tenants their own dedicated namespaces would cost roughly 5.3 times the storage of putting them all in one shared, filtered index -- almost entirely because of per-namespace fixed overhead rather than any difference in the actual vector data being stored, which is identical either way.

exercises.prompt: Write `route_tenant(tenant_id, tenant_vector_count, whale_threshold, num_shared_partitions)` that returns a dedicated namespace name for tenants at or above whale_threshold, and otherwise hashes the tenant into one of num_shared_partitions shared partitions using the given deterministic_hash function. Then route the four sample tenants below.
hints: Check tenant_vector_count against whale_threshold first -- if it's at or above the threshold, the tenant should never be hashed into a shared partition at all.
For non-whale tenants, deterministic_hash(tenant_id) % num_shared_partitions gives a stable partition number for that exact tenant_id, every time.
Return a formatted string in each branch -- f"dedicated_namespace:{tenant_id}" or f"shared_partition_{partition_number}".
exercises.solutionExplanation: tenant_y, at 2 million vectors, meets the whale_threshold of 1 million and is routed straight to its own dedicated_namespace:tenant_y, regardless of anything about its tenant_id string -- size alone decides that branch. tenant_x (500 vectors) and tenant_z (4000 vectors) both stay under the threshold, so each gets hashed via deterministic_hash(tenant_id) % 4 into one of the 4 shared partitions -- a stable, repeatable assignment based purely on the tenant_id's own characters, so the same tenant always lands in the same partition on every call, which matters for actually routing that tenant's future reads and writes consistently to the same physical location.

assessments.prompt: A tenant submits a GDPR-style erasure request. How does handling this request typically differ between a namespace-per-tenant deployment and a shared index relying on metadata filters and tombstones?
options: There is no real difference -- both approaches delete data with identical speed and guarantees.

Namespace-per-tenant lets you drop the entire namespace as a single atomic operation with no lingering data; the shared index approach requires tombstoning every one of the tenant's vectors and then relying on a compaction pass to physically purge them, leaving a window where the tombstoned data still physically exists.
Shared indexes cannot support data erasure at all, only namespace-per-tenant deployments can.
Namespace-per-tenant deployments require re-embedding all of a tenant's data before it can be erased.
assessments.explanation: Dropping a namespace is a single, atomic, immediately verifiable operation with no intermediate state where deleted data still exists physically. A shared index has to tombstone the tenant's vectors first (an immediate, cheap flag) and then wait for -- or explicitly trigger -- a compaction pass to actually reclaim the storage and remove the data from the underlying structure, which is correct in the end but has a real gap where the data is marked deleted but not yet physically purged. Option A ignores that gap entirely. Option C is wrong -- shared indexes fully support erasure, they just require an extra maintenance step (compaction) to complete it. Option D is a fabricated requirement with no basis -- erasure doesn't involve re-embedding anything.

assessments.prompt: A startup with 50,000 small tenants (averaging 200 vectors each) is deciding between giving each tenant a dedicated namespace or using one shared index with a tenant_id filter. Explain the tradeoffs and what you'd recommend, and how that recommendation might change if 20 of those tenants each have 50 million vectors.
assessments.modelAnswer: For 50,000 tenants averaging only 200 vectors each, dedicated namespaces are a poor default: every namespace pays a fixed baseline overhead (graph or cluster bookkeeping) independent of how many vectors it holds, and multiplying that fixed cost by 50,000 tenants produces a total footprint several times larger than a single shared index holding the exact same underlying vector data, purely from overhead that has nothing to do with the tenants' actual content. A shared index with a tenant_id metadata filter pays that fixed overhead once, amortized across all 50,000 tenants, and is also operationally simpler to run -- one index to build, tune, and monitor, rather than 50,000 independent ones, each of which needs its own maintenance (compaction, parameter tuning) to stay healthy. The tradeoff being accepted is a larger blast radius if a filtering bug ever slips through, and exposure to noisy-neighbor effects if any one tenant's traffic spikes -- both real risks, but ones that a single, well-tested filtering and monitoring pipeline can manage more reliably than the sheer operational surface area of 50,000 separate namespaces. Once 20 tenants each reach 50 million vectors, though, the calculation flips specifically for those 20: at that size, the same fixed per-namespace overhead is a rounding error next to their own data, so the storage argument for pooling them evaporates, while the isolation argument (bounding blast radius, avoiding noisy-neighbor contention from what are now genuinely large, high-traffic tenants, and giving them a clean atomic erasure path) becomes much stronger given how much traffic and data each one represents. The right recommendation isn't 'all namespaces' or 'all shared' -- it's a hybrid: keep the long tail of small tenants pooled in a shared index (or a modest number of hashed partitions), and carve out dedicated namespaces specifically for the 20 whale tenants whose size and traffic profile actually justify the operational cost of a separate namespace.
